In Figure 1(a), we ignore non-floating/pinning version constraints as they only occupy 0.83% of version constraints in our dataset. Bogart et al. 2021; Jafari et al. 2022; Raemaekers et al. 2017]. In a survey conducted in 2020, the majority of practitioners in the npm ecosystem were in favor of (semantic-versioning-based) floating [Jafari et al. 2022]. It is argued that pinning accumulates technical debt in the form of outdated dependencies [Hacker News 2018; Jafari et al. 2022], prevents security fixes from propagating downstream [Chinthanet et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2023], and increases the likelihood of dependency conflicts (or bloat in npm) [Hacker News 2017; StackOverflow 2017]. However, recent high-profile malicious package update incidents provide a new argument in favor of pinning, as pinning reduces the attack surface for malicious package updates. Given this argument, together with prior arguments that pinning increases application stability and reproducibility [Leiter 2023; Lucid 2017; Radzikowski 2021], many practitioners now argue in favor of pinning for security sensitive applications – for example, a survey of 17 domain experts and 134 software developers by Ladisa et al. [2023] ranks pinning as a top-3 safeguard against supply chain attacks in terms of utility/cost ratio; the OpenSSF Scorecard project [OpenSSF 2023; Zahan et al. 2023a] included “pinned dependencies” as one of its 18 security best practices. This discussion clearly reaches practitioners—as we show in Figure 1 (and explain in more depth later in Section 3.1), practitioners in npm have gradually shifted toward pinning more dependencies since 2020. Overall, controversies remain on whether the benefits of pinning outweigh its drawbacks, as manifested by online discussions [Bressers 2022; Curphey 2022; Renovate Bot 2018] and evidenced by the contradicting results from the collected practitioner opinions in prior studies [Jafari et al. 2022; Ladisa et al. 2023]. However, to the best of our knowledge, there is no quantitative evidence so far about the actual impact of pinning versus floating dependencies on the security and maintenance trade-ofs in Table 1. To gather quantitative evidence about pinning and floating, we perform a repository mining study on the npm ecosystem, the most frequently discussed ecosystem in the literature. Our study highlights an important complication that makes the discussion around pinning so dificult: Since a project can only control the version constraints of its direct dependencies, the actual impact of pinning as a local intervention is complicated and unclear, contingent upon both the decisions made upstream and the behaviors of dependency management tools. To measure this impact holistically from empirical data, we raise the following research question: • RQ1: (Impact ofPinning) How does the individual choice of pinning direct dependencies afect the overall security risks and maintenance costs in one’s own dependency graph? To answer this research question, we collect a large sample ofnpm packages and GitHub repositories using npm. Then, we use an experimental time-traveling feature of the npm dependency resolver to simulate the evolution of their dependency graphs over a 12-month period. We estimate the impact of pinning on a set of five security and maintenance-related metrics using fixed-efect panel regression [Brüderl and Ludwig 2015; Hanck et al. 2021]. A key (and counter-intuitive) finding from our model is that for the purpose of reducing the attack surface of malicious updates, pinning is futile and can be even harmful for projects with ≥498 direct and transitive dependencies (afecting 26% of GitHub repositories in our dataset). That is, pinning is inefective for one of its main goals, all while creating substantial costs for managing outdated, vulnerable, and conflicting dependencies. Inspired by this finding, we argue that ecosystem-level interventions (e.g., investing resources to secure critical open-source projects) are more efective than (possibly futile) local interventions of pinning direct dependencies to improve the overall resilience of an open-source ecosystem against malicious package updates. To empirically test this, we explore the second research question: • RQ2: (Ecosystem-Level Interventions) How efective is coordinating pinning among selected upstream packages in reducing the risk of malicious package updates ecosystem-wide? We answer this research question by simulating coordinated eforts in the entire npm dependency network. We formulate attack models and defense strategies in the dependency network, define heuristics to intervene in selected upstream packages, and measure the overall risk of malicious package updates after the intervention. Our findings indicate that it is possible to reduce the average spread of malicious package updates in the npm dependency network by nearly 30% if we pin in 100 intentionally selected important packages. However, as we will quantify, this intervention could be substantially more efective (up to 75%) if npm implements a new transitive pinning feature to allow packages to pass their entire pinned dependency graphs downstream. Summary ofContributions. Our paper contributes novel quantitative evidence on the security and maintenance impact of version constraints in a packaging ecosystem, especially in light of recent concerns about malicious package updates. Our findings align with the opinions of npm developers [Jafari et al. 2022] but contradict the views of security practitioners [Ladisa et al. 2023; Zahan et al. 2023a], suggesting that pinning direct dependencies is futile (and can be even counterproductive) as protection against malicious package updates. In addition, we contribute evidence that a new ecosystem-wide intervention, along with tooling changes and ecosystem-wide allocation of collectively pooled resources, can be an efective intervention against malicious package updates. Our findings lead to concrete advice for developers and ecosystem policy makers to improve the state of software supply chain security (Section 5).
